To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the use of the word "and" is a good predictor for the semantic relationship between two nouns in a compound; 2) the use of distributional information is a good predictor of the semantic relationship between nouns in a compound, and 3) combining distributional information and the presence of "and" in a compound is an effective method for classifying compound noun semantics.

(1) the semantic interpretation of compounds is highly context dependent, (2) a large number of compounds are polysemous and (3) the interpretation of compounds is influenced by the syntactic context in which they occur.
the use of a combination of lexical and relational information, in a kernel framework, is a promising approach to compound noun interpretation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods for the automatic analysis of the semantic relations in noun-noun constructions, with a focus on compounds.
the development and application of computational models for the semantic analysis of noun compounds and other noun-nou constructions.
the development of computational methods for analysing the semantics of noun-noun constructions, with an emphasis on compound nouns.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the compound nouns are a very interesting phenomenon and that they have a lot of potential for further studies.

the use of the word “compound” in the context of the present study is not justified, as the word “compound”, in the sense that it is used in the present study, is not a compound, in the sense that compounds have been defined in the present study.

, while the results are promising and show that the use of distributional kernels can be a powerful tool in the classification of semantic relations, the results also indicate that there is still much to be learned.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results of this thesis are a contribution to computational semantics and natural language processing.
we have shown the feasibility of using the distributional similarity paradigm for the analysis of noun-noun constructions, with a particular focus on compounds.
we have developed a novel approach to the problem of compound noun semantics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while there are many different ways to learn the meaning of a word from its context, there is no one best method.

the combination of lexical and relational similarity is an effective approach for the semantic classification of noun-noun constructions, and that this approach can be implemented using distributional kernels on probability distributions and sets of strings, respectively.
we have demonstrated that the use of distributional kernels can be an effective approach to learning compound noun semantics.
